title: Poggatacut, Sachem of the Manhassets of Shelter Island
summary: Poggatacut is remembered as a Manhansett sachem and Wyandanch’s older brother. Early accounts connect Shelter Island leadership with Gardiner, Hartford diplomacy, and the 1648 East Hampton agreement, while differing name identifications complicate the final years.
content:
Shelter Island and an influential family

Poggatacut was a Manhansett sachem associated with Shelter Island and remembered as the older brother of Wyandanch. Historical accounts connect him with the names Youghco and Yovawan, though the identifications are not uniform. His life belongs to the network of eastern Long Island leaders negotiating across the bays and Long Island Sound in the 1630s and 1640s.1 4

His birth date is unknown. Later histories commonly place his death in 1651, while accounts that equate him with the Yoco named in the 1652 Shelter Island purchase extend his activity into early 1653. Those differing identifications should not be turned into a falsely exact lifespan.1 4

1637: an elder consulted during the Pequot War

In his 1660 account of the Pequot War, Lion Gardiner recalled Wyandanch coming to Saybrook to ask about peace and trade. When Gardiner demanded that Long Islanders deliver the heads of Pequot refugees, Wyandanch said he would consult his older brother, the sachem living on Shelter Island.1

The passage shows the importance of consultation within Wyandanch’s family before making a dangerous wartime commitment. It also places Shelter Island within a conflict whose consequences crossed the Sound. Gardiner’s account reflects his own role and demands.1

May 3, 1639: Yovawan, Aswaw, and Gardiners Island

The Gardiners Island deed names Yovawan and his wife Aswaw as the Native parties conveying Manchonat to Lion Gardiner. The consideration recorded in the deed was ten coats of trading cloth. Aswaw’s inclusion makes this a family transaction, rather than a solitary male sachem’s bargain.1

In a letter printed with the deed, historian J. Hammond Trumbull suggested that Yovawan may have been Wyandanch’s elder brother, known to the English as Poggatacut. That is the basis for linking this document to Poggatacut’s biography; the deed itself uses Yovawan’s name.1

1644–1648: diplomacy and the East Hampton agreement

In September 1644, Youghco personally requested a certificate from the United Colonies commissioners at Hartford. It named him with Wiantause, Moughmaitow, and Weenagaminin and recorded friendship with English and Dutch settlers. The obligations included tribute and responsibility for addressing injuries.2 3

The April 29, 1648 East Hampton agreement names Poggatacut with Wyandanch, Momoweta, and Nowedonah. Its Native parties retained hunting, fishing, wampum-shell gathering, and a share of stranded whales. Their participation joined several local leadership networks in a transaction affecting the South Fork.2 3

1652: the Manhansetts defend their homes

The later Shelter Island dispute belongs to the history of his community even where the sachems’ names remain difficult to reconcile. On September 2, 1652, Cockenoe told the United Colonies commissioners that the island’s Native residents were being threatened with removal. They maintained that the land earlier given to James Forrett had been limited by marked trees and did not include surrendering their homes.4

A December 1652 agreement names Yoco, formerly Unkenchie, with other Native men. Read alongside the complaint, it reveals a community contesting the scope of a colonial title. The Manhansett story continued through these negotiations, rather than ending with a date assigned to one sachem.4

why_this_matters: Poggatacut keeps Manhanset leadership visible in Shelter Island history. His appearances in early records show Native diplomacy and land relationships before town histories narrowed the story to colonial settlement.
activity_update_summary: Expanded historical context, family and land connections, linked references, and dated Historic Moments.
